opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think refactoring is one of those things that sounds unglamorous, but it's where a huge amount of the real-world value is hiding.

If you look at how software actually gets built, most engineering time isn't spent writing shiny new things from scratch. It's spent living inside very large, very old code bases: systems that have accumulated decades of decisions, some good, some made under deadline pressure, some by people who left the company years ago. Everyone knows there's a better architecture in there somewhere. Everyone knows the migration they *should* do. But the cost is so high, and the risk of breaking something so real, that it just never happens. So you get this enormous amount of technical debt that the whole industry is quietly paying interest on.

What's exciting about AI here is that these are exactly the tasks that are hard for humans in an unrewarding way, and increasingly tractable for models. A large refactor is often thousands of small, mostly mechanical changes, each requiring some local understanding: what does this function really do, who calls it, what invariants does it rely on. A person can do any one of those, but doing ten thousand of them carefully, without losing focus, is brutal. A model that can hold context, reason about the code, run the tests, and iterate can grind through that with a level of consistency that's really hard for a human team to match.

And it changes the economics. Projects that were "someday, maybe" (migrating off a deprecated framework, untangling a monolith, moving to a new language, adding type safety across a code base) suddenly become things you can actually decide to do. That unlocks velocity for everything built on top. Cleaner code means faster future development, fewer bugs, easier onboarding. It compounds.

I also think it's a great proving ground for where these systems are going more broadly. Refactoring at scale forces the model to be genuinely agentic: understand a big system, make a plan, execute over a long horizon, verify its own work, and know when to ask a human. Those are the capabilities that matter far beyond code. So it's both immediately valuable and a window into what AI as a real collaborator looks like.

The way I think about it is that the goal isn't to replace the engineer's judgment. The engineer still decides *what* the system should look like. The AI makes it possible to actually get there. That's a pretty profound shift in what a single team can accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response says AI changes the economics and makes migrations more feasible, but it does not suggest that halving migration costs would cause ten times as many migrations.

r002.rationale: The response describes technical debt in large, old code bases, but does not identify continued dependence on COBOL systems as an accumulating liability.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer in character as the podcast guest, with no tools.

Because the bottleneck in software has never really been writing new code. It's dealing with the code that already exists. Every large company is sitting on tens of millions of lines that were written over a decade or two, by people who have mostly moved on, in frameworks and languages that are increasingly hard to hire for. And the honest truth is that almost nobody touches that stuff, because the risk is enormous and the payoff is invisible. Nobody gets promoted for migrating the billing system off a 2009 version of Java. So it just sits there, and it quietly taxes every single thing the organization tries to do.

What's changed is that this kind of work is almost perfectly suited to what these models are good at. A migration or a large refactor is usually not intellectually hard in the way inventing a new algorithm is hard. It's hard because it's vast, it's tedious, it's full of thousands of small decisions that all have to be consistent, and a human loses focus around the four hundredth file. A model doesn't get bored. You can give it the pattern, give it the tests, give it the ability to run the build, and let it grind through the whole thing while you review and course-correct. And critically, code is verifiable. You can compile it, you can run the test suite, you can diff the behavior. That tight feedback loop is exactly what makes it a domain where the model can actually be trusted to do real work rather than just suggest things.

So when I say it's a big opportunity, I mean it a few ways. For an individual company, it means projects that were literally on a "never" list suddenly become quarters instead of decades, and that unlocks velocity on everything downstream. At the industry level, I think a huge amount of global engineering effort is tied up in maintenance that produces no new value, and freeing even a fraction of that is a real change in how much software humanity can produce. And honestly, for the models themselves, it's one of the most useful places to learn. Refactoring at scale teaches a system about how real codebases are actually structured, how changes ripple, what breaks. That's the kind of grounded, high-volume, checkable work that makes the next generation of these tools better at everything else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses migrations becoming faster and enabling more work, but it does not say that halving their cost could cause ten times as many migrations.

r002.rationale: The response describes legacy code as a quiet tax and mentions old Java, but it does not identify continued dependence on COBOL systems.

astra-6.text:
Because there’s this huge gap between knowing how you’d like your codebase to work and actually being able to get it there. If you’re starting from scratch, you can choose a clean architecture. But in a large, existing system, you’ve got years of decisions embedded in it. Changing one abstraction might mean touching thousands of places, and it’s hard to justify that investment when you also have features to ship.

AI can potentially change the economics of that work. You can describe the transformation you want, have it help work through the changes, and use tests and review to check that the behavior is preserved. The hard part is making sure it understands the exceptions and the dependencies—you don’t want something that just produces a plausible-looking diff.

What’s exciting is that maintenance can become much more continuous. Instead of accumulating complexity because cleaning it up is too expensive, you can keep bringing the codebase closer to the design you actually want. That makes every subsequent change easier, too.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could change the economics of refactoring, but does not state that halving migration costs could lead to ten times as many migrations.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention COBOL systems or describe continued dependence on them as an accumulating liability.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in a large codebase, a change that’s simple to describe can be incredibly expensive to carry out. You want to replace an old interface, or change how some data is represented, but that decision touches thousands of places. Someone has to understand the dependencies, make all those changes, and verify that the behavior still holds together.

AI can help close that gap between knowing what you want to change and actually being able to do it. You can work through the code, update the callers, run the tests, and iterate. You still need good judgment about the design and strong ways to check correctness, but the mechanical scope becomes much less of a barrier.

That’s exciting because it changes which improvements are worth attempting. Teams accumulate technical debt partly because fixing it would take too much time away from everything else. If you can bring that cost down substantially, you can keep improving the foundations of the software while continuing to build on it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can substantially reduce the cost of refactoring and make more improvements worth attempting, but it does not communicate halving the cost or ten times as many migrations.

r002.rationale: The response discusses technical debt generally and does not identify continued dependence on COBOL systems as an accumulating liability.
